gist: Macro strategist Henrik Zeberg argues the current Bitcoin rally to a targeted $115-120K is a bear-market 'fool's rally,' not a new bull cycle, and expects a subsequent crash of roughly 90% once a US recession (driven by a collapsing labor market and a bursting AI capex bubble) forces the dollar sharply higher.

insights.claim: Henrik Zeberg's standing call is that Bitcoin rallies to roughly $115,000-$120,000, gets rejected a second time near that level, and then is crushed in a broader bear market rather than continuing a new bull run.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Traders treating the current rally as the start of a new multi-year bull cycle risk being caught in a distribution top near $115-120K; watch for a second failed attempt at that level as the trigger to de-risk.
insights.quote: My call has been for Bitcoin to go to 115 120,000 again and then you're going to see it actually, you know, getting rejected a second time around that level and then you see going to be uh be crushed.

insights.claim: Zeberg expects Bitcoin's eventual crash to be proportionally worse than the NASDAQ's, projecting roughly a 90% decline for Bitcoin versus an expected 60-70%+ NASDAQ correction in the coming recession, since Bitcoin historically corrects more than the NASDAQ in downturns.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Sizing crypto exposure for a garden-variety drawdown could be a major miscalculation if a real recession hits; a 90% Bitcoin retracement is a tail scenario worth explicit hedging or exit planning.
insights.quote: I would not expect Bitcoin to to correct in less. I think it will correct even more. I think it'll be like 90%.

insights.claim: Zeberg dismisses the popular Bitcoin four-year halving cycle theory as unreliable pattern-matching, comparing it to astrology, and instead analyzes Bitcoin through cross-asset ratios and macro business-cycle phasing.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Investors anchoring Bitcoin allocation decisions purely on the halving-cycle calendar may be relying on a framework the analyst considers structurally meaningless once macro conditions (dollar, liquidity, recession risk) diverge from prior cycles.
insights.quote: I mean, stop that. That's like astrology for for for the uh for the markets, right?

insights.claim: Using a Bitcoin-to-S&P 500 ratio (to strip out dollar effects) shows Bitcoin's current strength resembles late 2021: a sharp rally and new nominal all-time high that nonetheless failed to make a new high versus the S&P, which Zeberg reads as confirmation of a bear-market rally rather than a genuine new bull market.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Watch the BTC/SPX ratio, not just Bitcoin's dollar price, for confirmation of trend strength; a nominal new high with a lower ratio high is a classic bear-rally signature.

insights.claim: Zeberg's framework holds that Bitcoin rallies require three conditions simultaneously: a risk-on market environment, sufficient liquidity, and a dollar that is not too strong, making crypto the most demanding ('difficult child') of all risk assets to time.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Use this three-factor checklist (risk appetite, liquidity, dollar direction) as a go/no-go filter before adding Bitcoin exposure rather than relying on price momentum alone.
insights.quote: it's like the uh the difficult child there amongst all the risk assets.

insights.claim: Zeberg's standing macro thesis is that the US Dollar Index (DXY) declines further to about 93-94 before reversing and strengthening sharply, even as market narratives at that point will be calling for continued 'dollar death.'
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A DXY bottom near 93-94 followed by a sharp reversal is the trigger event to watch; a subsequent dollar rally would flip the macro backdrop against risk assets, especially crypto.
insights.quote: this has been my standing thesis for some time that the dollar is going to decline and we're going to see 93 94 on the Dixie.

insights.claim: Zeberg argues Bitcoin rallies are only sustainable while the DXY stays below roughly 100-105; if the dollar were to climb back toward 110-120, it would effectively end any Bitcoin/crypto rally for a prolonged period.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Track DXY as a leading macro gauge for crypto positioning: sustained moves above ~100-105 would be a red flag, and a run to 110-120 would be treated as an outright bear signal for the entire asset class.
insights.quote: everything here any Bitcoin rally would need to see that bit that the dollar does not rise above 100 105. If it does that we have seen again and again that Bitcoin does not do well.

themes.theme: Narrative Traps: ETFs, Clarity Act, and News Catalysts

insights.claim: Zeberg frames news catalysts (e.g., Treasury Secretary Bessent's doubling of T-bill issuance and the White House crypto summit on the day Bitcoin broke out) as mere triggers ('the skier on the avalanche slope'), not root causes -- the real driver was a pre-existing structural rotation of capital from equities/AI stocks into crypto that had already been building for weeks.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Don't overweight single news headlines as the 'reason' for a move; instead track underlying capital-rotation structure (equities to crypto lag of 10-20 weeks) which is the more durable, tradeable signal.
insights.quote: It could have been any event like it could have been any event that made the avalanche bumble down the mountain slide side.

insights.claim: Zeberg cites the original Bitcoin ETF launch as a cautionary precedent: the market widely expected the ETF to unlock institutional capital and push prices higher, but the ETF approval instead coincided almost exactly with a market top and subsequent decline.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Treat consensus 'this catalyst will bring in new capital' narratives with skepticism -- the anticipated flows may already be front-run into the market well before the official event.
insights.quote: What did we see? That was actually the time where we saw the top in Bitcoin and we saw a decline.

insights.claim: Zeberg expects the pending Clarity Act (US crypto market-structure legislation) to follow the same 'buy the rumor, sell the news' pattern as the Bitcoin ETF: capital anticipating the approval may already be positioned, so the real economy's weakness could dominate once the news is out rather than triggering a fresh leg of adoption-driven upside.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Fade the consensus expectation that Clarity Act passage alone extends the crypto rally; the macro backdrop (labor market, dollar) will likely matter more than the legislative catalyst.
insights.quote: everybody expects that the Clarity Act if when it gets approved or you know go through is going to bring a lot of capital into the markets. What if that capital is already running in there now

insights.claim: Zeberg cites the revised non-farm payrolls data showing average job creation of only about 16,000 per month over the trailing year, with the 12-month moving average around 50,000 -- a level historically only seen in or near a US recession (recession periods typically show ~80,000-100,000 on that same moving average).
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: This payrolls trend is the analyst's core evidence the US economy is already in a de facto growth recession, undercutting bullish 'strong economy' narratives used to justify risk-asset valuations.
insights.quote: job creation as I said for the last year which was revised here was 16,000 per month. It is incredibly weak.

insights.claim: Zeberg flags that the most recent monthly jobs report had only a 44% survey response rate, with the remaining 56% of respondents statistically imputed as performing similarly to the 44% who did respond, raising doubts about the reliability of the headline job-creation figure.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Headline payroll beats/misses should be discounted given known survey response-rate degradation; wait for revisions rather than trading the initial print.
insights.quote: I don't trust the 162 we got just the other day because that was a 44% response rate.

insights.claim: Zeberg notes labor force participation is collapsing, with roughly 2-3 million people exiting the ~170-172 million US labor force since October of the prior year, alongside long-term unemployment duration at its highest level in 50-60 years outside of an official recession.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Discouraged-worker dropout and rising long-term unemployment duration are classic pre-recession slack indicators masked by a flattering headline unemployment rate.
insights.quote: it's like two and a 2.2 two three million people that have left since October last year.

insights.claim: Zeberg states that over 60% (he cites ~66%) of US consumers live paycheck to paycheck, and the median US consumer cannot absorb an unexpected $2,000 expense, leaving consumption highly vulnerable to any further softening in employment.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: This fragility is the transmission mechanism from any job-market wobble to a consumption-driven GDP slowdown, since consumption is ~68-70% of US GDP.
insights.quote: The median consumer in the US cannot afford a $2,000 extra expense. $2,000. That's your car breaking down.

insights.claim: Zeberg explicitly disagrees with a prior podcast guest's thesis that reaccelerating inflation will force Fed rate hikes that function as quasi-QE (via banks refinancing rolled-over government debt), arguing instead that the labor market data does not support an inflation-reacceleration case.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Positions built around an 'inflation forces hikes, hikes become disguised QE' thesis are, in Zeberg's view, mis-specified; he sees the Fed eventually cutting in response to labor weakness, not hiking.

insights.claim: Zeberg argues the US household savings rate of only 2-3% today (versus 10-20% in the 1970s) means consumers lack the spare capacity to keep spending through price shocks (e.g., an oil price spike), so inflation cannot become self-reinforcing the way it did in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: This undercuts the '1970s-style inflation redux' narrative used to justify higher-for-longer rate expectations, and instead supports a deflationary/disinflationary bias for policy going forward.
insights.quote: The savings rate in the 1970s was between 10 10 and 20%. That means that people actually had the extra money in the pocket when they when when inflation was going up and they spent that money extra.

insights.claim: Zeberg cites real-time inflation trackers (Trueflation) showing current inflation closer to about 2.2%, well below the narrative of persistently high inflation, and notes official CPI-style data is lagging and based on what he calls incomplete methodology.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: If real-time inflation is running near 2%, the case for the Fed holding or hiking rates is much weaker than consensus assumes, supporting a base case of eventual rate cuts.
insights.quote: inflation is probably if you do it on a you know real-time basis more like 2.2% or something like that at this point

insights.claim: Zeberg argues liquidity injections cannot fix an underlying solvency problem, pointing out that the Fed cut rates aggressively into the 2008 financial crisis (125 basis points in January 2008 alone, cutting continuously from June 2007 into 2009) and the crisis happened anyway once the consumer pulled back.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Rebuts the popular 'liquidity/M2 always rescues risk assets' thesis; investors relying on expected Fed easing to backstop equities/crypto should note that easing did not prevent the 2008 crash once consumer-driven insolvency set in.
insights.quote: Why did we have a financial crisis if that was the case? If if liquidity could sell solve it, why did we see the market go belly up?

insights.claim: Zeberg argues AI adoption is a near-term macro drag despite long-term productivity benefits, because firms now need fewer employees for the same or greater output (illustrated by the host's own company hiring fewer staff while raising output), which reduces aggregate consumption -- 68-70% of GDP -- even as AI capex itself has been propping up job creation and GDP.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Expect a multi-year (Zeberg suggests roughly 2-5 years) transition drag on consumption-driven growth from AI-linked headcount reduction before productivity gains show up positively in the economy; this is a structural headwind, not a one-off.
insights.quote: If you're not going to hire in two people any longer, but only one, and everybody else does that, why is that good for consumption? It is bad for consumption.

insights.claim: Zeberg notes US capacity utilization has fallen to about 76%, meaning businesses on average are sitting on roughly 30% surplus capacity, which removes any near-term incentive to hire even amid the AI investment boom.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Low capacity utilization alongside heavy AI capex spending suggests the AI buildout is running ahead of actual end-demand, a classic overinvestment pattern that historically precedes a capex bust.
insights.quote: the capacity utilization in the US right now is down to 76% 76% so all most businesses have like 30% extra surplus capacity on a on an average basis

insights.claim: Zeberg calls current AI capex spending a 'clear bubble,' comparable in structure to the dot-com and telecom overbuild cycles, and warns that if it bursts it would create a dollar liquidity shortage that would be severely negative for crypto specifically.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A cracking AI capex cycle is flagged as a distinct, separate risk trigger (beyond the labor-market/recession thesis) for a dollar squeeze that would hit crypto disproportionately hard.
insights.quote: there will be a lack for dollars and the lack for dollars are going to kill anything that has to do with crypto for so for quite a foreseeable future.

insights.claim: Zeberg says his proprietary macro-phase model, built on close to 1 million data points comparing historical economic phases, finds the current environment most closely resembles Q4 1999 -- the euphoric blow-off phase right before the dot-com top.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: The 1999-2000 analog implies markets can still melt up sharply for a short window before a violent reversal, so tactical bulls should be watching for the same speed-of-reversal risk that hit NASDAQ in 2000.
insights.quote: we can see that this the phase we have right here is resembling 1999 Q4 the most and this is based on close to 1 million data points.

insights.claim: Zeberg expects the NASDAQ to rally another 25-30% before topping, drawing a direct parallel to early 2000 when the index rallied 44% in its final seven weeks and then crashed 40% in just three to four weeks; he flags roughly the 37,000-39,000 NASDAQ level as around where the top could form.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: A specific price zone (37K-39K on the NASDAQ) and a blow-off-then-crash pattern give traders a concrete level and shape to watch for a top, rather than an open-ended melt-up assumption.
insights.quote: in 2000 over the last seven weeks you saw that the stock market was rallying 44%. 44% in seven weeks... at then we saw it that the top was in and then it crashed and it crashed by 40% in 3 to four weeks.

insights.claim: Zeberg's key reversal signal to watch is short-term bond yields: after the current normal late-cycle rise in yields, a sharp reversal and decline in short-term yields would mark the point where 'the clock really starts' toward a market top; he also says his own proprietary coincident indicator already turned negative in early July.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Use a sharp drop in short-term yields (following the current late-cycle rise) as a concrete, monitorable trigger for rotating out of risk assets ahead of the broader top.
insights.quote: I think we are very very very close to that point where you see the reversal in the short-term yields first and you start to see that they will drop rather strongly and when that happens then the clock is really starting

insights.claim: Zeberg's positioning framework: for a 5+ year horizon, he favors gold and silver even accepting near-term dollar-related weakness, because they should outperform most other assets on a relative basis through the coming downturn; for a 3-6 month horizon he expects a difficult whipsaw (chase the blow-off top in NASDAQ/Bitcoin, then flip to bonds/US Treasuries as safe havens once the selloff hits, before an eventual Fed intervention resets the regime again).
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: This gives a horizon-based playbook: long-term investors can rotate toward precious metals now, while short-term traders should plan an exit from the current risk-asset melt-up before rotating into bonds/Treasuries ahead of Fed intervention.
insights.quote: if you say I don't care what happens the next 5 years I will say then buy gold silver and whatever at this point

insights.claim: Zeberg cites the US housing market as another sign of underlying weakness: existing home sales relative to population are at their lowest level ever recorded without unemployment being above 8-10%, notable because housing (with its multiplier effects on related spending) makes up roughly 25% of the US economy.
insights.speaker: Henrik Zeberg
insights.so_what: Housing transaction volume, not just prices, is flashing a recessionary signal well before unemployment has risen -- a leading indicator investors can track independently of the jobs data debate.
insights.quote: the number of h homes existing homes sold to population it has never been this low without having an unemployment above 8 10%.
